T-money is a rechargeable transit card sold at convenience stores (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven) and subway station kiosks for a small card fee.

1. It works on subway, city buses, and many taxis nationwide — tap in and tap out, transfers between subway and bus within the transfer window are discounted.
2. Balance and recharge are done with cash or card at convenience stores or station machines; unused balance can be partially refunded before leaving Korea.

Korea is largely cashless in cities — most cafes, convenience stores, and restaurants accept card, including foreign Visa/Mastercard, though small traditional markets and some rural spots may be cash-only.

1. Airport and city-center ATMs marked 'Global' or with a foreign card logo accept international cards; look for Woori, KEB Hana, or 7-Eleven ATMs for the most reliable acceptance.
2. Notify your bank of your travel dates beforehand to avoid a card freeze on first use.

Late-night pharmacies do exist but aren't as common as 24-hour convenience stores — look for a green cross sign, and ask staff or a hotel front desk for the nearest one open after hours.

1. Common over-the-counter medicine names differ from Western brands, so showing the pharmacist a translated symptom list (Papago works well) speeds things up.
2. Travel insurance is worth having, since upfront payment is usually required before any reimbursement process at Korean hospitals.

Most tourists lose their Tax Free refund before they even reach the airport — not from missing paperwork, but from where they packed the item.

1. Tourists spending over the minimum threshold at Tax Free-affiliated stores can reclaim VAT paid on purchases.
2. Ask for a Tax Free receipt/form at checkout, keep the item unused, and process the refund at airport kiosks (self-service or counter) before checking in your luggage if the item goes in checked baggage.
3. Refund percentage varies by amount spent; check the current threshold and rate before your trip since these are adjusted periodically.

The weather, not the crime rate, is what actually disrupts trips to Korea — and most itineraries build in zero buffer for it.

1. Natural events like typhoons (summer/early fall) or heavy snow (winter) can disrupt trains and flights with little warning — build a buffer day into your itinerary if traveling during those seasons.
2. Save the emergency numbers 112 (police) and 119 (fire/medical) before you land; many operators have English support.
3. Hotels and hostels can usually help translate in a pinch if you're unsure whether a situation needs official help.

Coin lockers at Korean subway stations look reliable — until you actually need one on a weekend. They fill fast during holidays. Luggage counters near Myeongdong/Hongdae hold bags all day flat-rate. Ever come up empty on lockers?
topic: Insadong traditional culture street

text:
Coin lockers aren't the guaranteed backup plan they look like in Korea. 🧳

1. Available at most major stations, payable with T-money — but they fill up fast on weekends and holidays.
2. Luggage storage counters near Myeongdong and Hongdae hold bags for a full day at a flat rate.
3. Some hotels will hold your bags even after checkout at no extra charge.
4. Always ask your hotel first before paying for outside storage.

Save this before your last day in Seoul.

Buses cost less than KTX/SRT and reach towns the trains skip — but take meaningfully longer. Worth it when your destination isn't near a station, or schedule matters more than an hour saved. Train or bus — what's your default?

This mistake costs people real money — and they don't find out until it's too late. High-speed rail isn't automatically the right call for every Korea trip. 🚌

2. They take meaningfully longer on the same routes, though.
3. Worth it when your destination isn't near a station, or flexibility matters more than an hour saved.
4. Underestimating a bus's buffer time is an easy mistake for tight connections.

text:
This mistake costs people real money — and they don't find out until it's too late.

The gesture that reads as rude to older Koreans isn't loud — it's handing over your card with one hand or a pointing finger. Both hands, or a supporting arm, reads well. Pour for others at a shared meal. Knew the two-hands rule?

📖 More on the blog — link in bio.

This mistake costs people real money — and they don't find out until it's too late. One small gesture quietly matters to older Koreans more than most first-timers realize. 🙇

1. Passing money or a card with one hand, or pointing with a single finger, can read as slightly rude.
2. Using both hands, or supporting your arm, is well received.
3. It's common to pour drinks for others rather than yourself at a shared meal.
4. Wait for the eldest or host to start eating first.

Save this before your first meal out in Korea.

Everyone assumes this works the same as back home. It doesn't.

Korea feels cash-optional until you hit a market that only takes cash — and by then it's too late. Most city spots take foreign cards, but traditional markets can be cash-only. Look for 'Global' ATMs. Ever gotten caught cash-less?

📖 More on the blog — link in bio.

Everyone assumes this works the same as back home. It doesn't. Korea feels cash-optional — until it very much isn't. 💵

1. Most cafes, convenience stores, and restaurants in cities accept foreign Visa/Mastercard.
2. Small traditional markets and some rural spots can be cash-only.
3. Look for 'Global' ATMs — Woori, KEB Hana, or 7-Eleven — for reliable international card withdrawals.
4. Notify your bank of your travel dates beforehand to avoid a card freeze.

Save this before your market day.

There's one detail that trips up almost every first-timer.

Convenience stores never close in Korea. Pharmacies do, and most travelers find out the hard way. Look for a green cross sign after hours, or ask your hotel. A Papago symptom list speeds up the counter. Knew pharmacies closed early?

📖 More on the blog — link in bio.

There's one detail that trips up almost every first-timer. Convenience stores never close in Korea. Pharmacies do — and it catches people off guard. 💊

1. 24-hour pharmacies are far less common than 24-hour convenience stores.
2. Look for a green cross sign, or ask staff or your hotel front desk for one open after hours.
3. A translated symptom list on Papago speeds up the counter conversation, since medicine names differ from Western brands.
4. Travel insurance is worth having, since upfront payment is usually required before reimbursement at Korean hospitals.

Save this before you need a late-night pharmacy.

Nobody tells you this before you land.

Google Maps quietly stops working the moment you land in Korea — most first-timers find out once they're lost. Naver Map or KakaoMap handle transit far better. Papago nails menu translation. Which app rescued your trip?

📖 More on the blog — link in bio.

Nobody tells you this before you land. Google Maps has a blind spot the moment you land in Korea. 🗺️

1. Naver Map or KakaoMap work far better for walking and transit directions here — Google's local data is limited.
2. Papago handles Korean translation naturally, including camera translation for menus and signs.
3. Kakao T is the go-to app for calling taxis reliably, especially late at night.
4. Download all three before you land, not after you're already lost.

The season that looks easiest to pack for in Korea usually catches travelers off guard. Summer means a July monsoon — pack an umbrella, not a raincoat. Winter outside Seoul needs real layers. Which season are you flying in?

📖 More on the blog — link in bio.

Most tourists get this wrong in their first hour. The 'easy' season to pack for in Korea is usually the one that surprises people most. 🌦️

1. Summer (Jun-Aug): hot and humid with a distinct monsoon season in July — pack light, breathable clothing and a compact umbrella.
2. Winter (Dec-Feb): dry and cold with occasional heavy snow, especially outside Seoul.
3. Spring and fall: the most comfortable seasons for walking-heavy days, but also the most crowded.

Save this before you pack for Korea.

1. Summer (Jun-Aug): hot and humid with a distinct monsoon season in July — pack light, breathable clothing and a compact umbrella.
2. Winter (Dec-Feb): dry and cold with occasional heavy snow, especially outside Seoul.
3. Spring and fall: the most comfortable seasons for walking-heavy days, but also the most crowded.

text:
Most visitors hand their T-money card back to nobody and just fly home with the balance on it — but unused T-money balance can be partially refunded before you leave Korea. 🇰🇷

1. Where to get one: convenience stores (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven) and subway station kiosks, for a small card fee.
2. Where it works: subway, city buses, and many taxis nationwide — not just Seoul.
3. How to use it: tap in AND tap out. Transfers between subway and bus inside the transfer window are discounted.
4. Topping up: cash or card at a convenience store counter or a station machine.
5. Leaving: ask for the refund on the unused balance before you go, not after.

Checklist to remember: buy at a convenience store → tap in, tap out → keep top-ups small in your final days → cash out the balance before the airport.

1. Alcohol is banned in national parks, so the old image of makgeolli at the summit no longer applies inside park boundaries, and cooking or open flames are restricted to designated areas.
2. National parks also close selected trails during spring and autumn wildfire-prevention periods and in winter for safety, so check the Korea National Park Service site or signage at the trailhead before committing to a route.
3. Most trailheads have restrooms and a cluster of restaurants serving pajeon, tofu stew and bibimbap for the post-hike meal, which is half the point for locals.

Korean street signs can spell the same place two different ways — and it's not a typo.

Revised Romanization is the modern standard, but older McCune-Reischauer spellings still show up everywhere.

The same syllable can appear as 'gim' or 'kim,' 'Busan' or 'Pusan,' depending on the sign's age.

Learning a few address terms like -ro (road), -gil (street), and -dong (neighborhood) helps a lot.

1. Tourists spending over the minimum threshold at Tax Free-affiliated stores can reclaim VAT paid on purchases.
2. Ask for a Tax Free receipt/form at checkout, keep the item unused, and process the refund at airport kiosks (self-service or counter) before checking in your luggage if the item goes in checked baggage.
3. Refund percentage varies by amount spent; check the current threshold and rate before your trip since these are adjusted periodically.

Do you tip in Korea? Short answer: no.

At most restaurants, cafes, taxis and salons, pay exactly what's on the bill. Extra cash can confuse staff.

Watch out:
• "Service" on a receipt usually means a free extra.
• Some upscale and hotel restaurants add a 10% service charge (about 21% with VAT). It's already included.

Save this for your next trip 📌

Locals do this differently than every blog post says.

Google Maps can show you subway and bus routes in Korea, but it can't give full driving or detailed walking directions, because national law restricts exporting precise mapping data to overseas servers.

Locals use Naver Map or Kakao Map instead, both of which have English interfaces and are far more accurate for walking, bus arrivals, and indoor subway exits.

Business hours, menus, and 'currently open' info are also much more reliable on the Korean apps, since that's where shops actually register themselves.

The guidebooks skip this part entirely.

Sorting recyclables isn't what actually trips people up in Korea — it's using the wrong bag.

General waste has to go into an official, district-specific bag (종량제 봉투, sold at local convenience stores and supermarkets); bags bought in a different district aren't accepted even if they look identical, since the collection fee is built into that specific bag's price.

This catches foreign residents and short-term renters far more than tourists in hotels, since nobody hands you the local bag with your key.
